passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: For most of the twentieth century, archaeologists agreed that the first people to reach the Americas were the makers of the Clovis culture, who spread across North America around thirteen thousand years ago. Their presence is marked by a distinctive fluted stone spear point, found at sites from the Plains to the East Coast. Claims of older, "pre-Clovis" settlement surfaced from time to time, but on close inspection the supposed tools or dates tended not to hold up. On this view, the Clovis horizon is not merely the earliest well-documented culture; it marks the moment of human arrival itself.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: The Clovis-first model has come under sustained pressure. At Monte Verde, in southern Chile, excavators have recovered wooden tools, hearths, and plant remains from layers securely dated to roughly a thousand years before the Clovis horizon. Other sites in both Americas have yielded comparable early dates. The difficulty for the older model is partly geographic: a settlement in southern Chile that predates Clovis cannot be reached from a North American point of first arrival in the time the model allows. The spread of such sites suggests that people were already widely established before Clovis points appeared.

question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument presented in Text 1?

choices.text: It would concede that no site predating Clovis has ever been securely dated and recommend setting the whole question aside until a clearly older site is finally found and confirmed.
Sites such as Monte Verde contain securely dated artifacts centuries older than the Clovis horizon, so that horizon cannot mark the first human arrival.
Clovis points do mark the earliest human presence, and their rapid spread across North America shows how quickly the first arrivals moved.
The disagreement matters only for North America, since the peopling of South America followed an entirely separate route.

explanation: The correct answer is B. Text 1 holds that the Clovis horizon marks the moment humans first reached the Americas, since older claims have not held up; Text 2 points to securely dated pre-Clovis material at Monte Verde and elsewhere and concludes that the Clovis horizon cannot be the arrival point. Choice B states that response. Choice A has Text 2 deny that any pre-Clovis site is securely dated, which is the opposite of its central evidence. Choice C endorses the Clovis-first view Text 2 rejects, and choice D limits the dispute to North America, whereas Text 2's strongest evidence is precisely a South American site.
